A program runs this code:

`colors = ["red", "blue", "green"]`
`print(colors[2])`
`print(colors[0])`
`print(colors[1])`

Arrange the printed lines in the order they appear.

help.hint_1: Positive indexes count from the beginning; negative indexes count from the end.

course-introduction.title: Welcome to Python Data & Functions
course-introduction.bodyMarkdown:
This course begins after the introductory Python course. You should already be comfortable with **variables, strings, input and output, conditionals, loops, and basic Python syntax**.

Now your programs will start working with collections of related values instead of handling everything one value at a time. You will learn how lists, tuples, and dictionaries organize data; how functions turn repeated logic into reusable tools; and how files let programs read, clean, and save information.

We begin with lists because they introduce the key idea behind this module: **one variable can hold an ordered collection of values**.

list-creation-basics.title: Creating lists
list-creation-basics.bodyMarkdown:
A **list** stores multiple values in one ordered collection. In Python, a list literal uses square brackets, with commas between the items.

```python
colors = ["red", "blue", "green"]
print(colors)
```

Output:

```text
['red', 'blue', 'green']
```

The important pieces are:

- `colors` is the variable that holds the list.
- `[` and `]` mark the beginning and end of the list.
- Commas separate the items.
- The items keep the order in which you place them.

A list can also be built from values already stored in variables.

```python
morning = "math"
afternoon = "science"
classes = [morning, afternoon]
print(classes)
```

Output:

```text
['math', 'science']
```

Here, Python uses the values inside `morning` and `afternoon` as the two list items.

indexing-basics.title: Reading items by index
indexing-basics.bodyMarkdown:
An **index** is the position Python uses to find an item in a list. Python starts counting at **0**.

```python
animals = ["cat", "dog", "fox"]
print(animals[0])
print(animals[1])
print(animals[2])
```

Output:

```text
cat
dog
fox
```

For this list:

| Item | Position in the list | Python index |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `"cat"` | first | `0` |
| `"dog"` | second | `1` |
| `"fox"` | third | `2` |

A common mistake is to use index `1` for the first item. In Python, index `1` means the **second** item.

Worked example:

```python
prices = [12, 15, 9, 20]
print(prices[2])
```

This prints `9` because index `2` points to the third item.

Indexes must refer to a real position. For example, `animals[3]` would raise an `IndexError` because this three-item list only has indexes `0`, `1`, and `2`.

negative-indexes.title: Reading from the end
negative-indexes.bodyMarkdown:
Python also lets you count backward from the end of a list with **negative indexes**.

```python
tasks = ["email", "report", "meeting", "backup"]
print(tasks[-1])
print(tasks[-2])
```

Output:

```text
backup
meeting
```

Negative indexes work from right to left:

- `-1` means the last item.
- `-2` means the second-to-last item.
- `-3` means the third-to-last item.

This is useful when you care about the end of a list but do not want to calculate its final positive index.
